---
title: "Performance and caching"
---

A session pays two fixed costs before its first prediction, the download of the weights from
Hugging Face and the JAX compilation of the network. The compilation is paid again for each new
batch size. Prediction itself is far cheaper than either.

## Setup cost

`preload_models` loads the three estiMINT gradient-boosted models and both stateMINT
checkpoints, downloading them if they are not already cached.

```{python}
import time
from estimint import preload_models

t0 = time.perf_counter()
eir_models, emulator_models = preload_models()
print(f"preload_models: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
print("estiMINT :", list(eir_models))
print("stateMINT:", list(emulator_models))
```

Call it once at the top of a script. On a cold machine most of that time is the download, roughly
38 MB per predictor. On a warm one it is deserialisation from disk. `preload_models` tracks
`main` rather than a pinned tag, so load the checkpoints yourself with
[`from_pretrained(..., revision=...)`](the-emulator.qmd) when the exact weights matter.

## The cache

Weights land in the standard Hugging Face cache.

```{python}
from huggingface_hub import constants

print(constants.HF_HUB_CACHE)
```

Two environment variables control the cache. Both must be set before the first import.

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `HF_HOME` | Relocates the whole cache. Point it at a shared or scratch filesystem on a cluster, where a home directory quota will not hold 80 MB of weights. |
| `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` | Forbids network access. Loads succeed from the cache and fail loudly otherwise. Set it on a compute node with no outbound route, and pre-populate the cache from the login node. |

```bash
export HF_HOME=/scratch/$USER/hf
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
```

## Batching

`.predict` is a single compiled forward pass over the whole batch, and JAX compiles the network
on first use and recompiles it whenever the batch size changes.

```{python}
import numpy as np
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

prevalence = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

district = {
    "eir": 31.96, "dn0_use": 0.311, "dn0_future": 0.485,
    "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0,
    "routine": 0.0, "itn_use": 0.70, "irs_use": 0.0,
    "itn_future": 0.70, "irs_future": 0.0, "lsm": 0.0,
}

batch = [dict(district, eir=float(e)) for e in np.linspace(5, 60, 50)]
len(batch)
```

The first call pays the compilation cost. The second does not.

```{python}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
prevalence.predict(batch)
first = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
prevalence.predict(batch)
second = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"first call  (compile + run): {first * 1000:7.0f} ms")
print(f"second call (run only)     : {second * 1000:7.0f} ms")
```

The same fifty scenarios then run as fifty separate calls, each compiled for a batch of one.

```{python}
prevalence.predict([district])          # pay the batch-of-one compilation

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for scenario in batch:
    prevalence.predict([scenario])
looped = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"one call, 50 scenarios : {second * 1000:7.0f} ms   ({second / 50 * 1000:.1f} ms each)")
print(f"50 calls, 1 scenario   : {looped * 1000:7.0f} ms   ({looped / 50 * 1000:.1f} ms each)")
print(f"speed-up               : {looped / second:.1f}x")
```

A call enters the compiled forward pass once, whatever the batch size. The loop pays it fifty
times over.

Build the whole list first, then call `.predict` once. A grid of a few hundred rows is still a
single call, and still under a second. The timings above came off whatever machine rendered the
cells, so trust the ratio rather than the absolute milliseconds.

## CPU and GPU

The timings above are CPU timings, and a CPU is adequate at the scale of a scenario grid, since
the emulator is small, two Mamba2 layers with `d_model` 256. On a GPU the same forward pass is
roughly six times faster, measured on an NVIDIA L40S, and both sit orders of magnitude below the
minutes a `malariasimulation` run of the same twelve simulated years takes. The measurements, and
what the speed costs in accuracy, are in [Accuracy and speed](../03-concepts/validation.qmd).

For a sweep of thousands of scenarios, a CUDA 12 build of JAX is available as an extra.

```bash
pip install "mintstate[gpu]"
```

Nothing in the API changes when a GPU is present. JAX places the computation on the accelerator
if it finds one, and without a CUDA-enabled JAX it falls back to CPU and warns, which is the only
sign the GPU is not in use.
